Chapter 4: Designing the Ideal Week—Intentional Planning and Scheduling
Now that you’ve got your priorities and strengths in focus, let’s talk about how you can actually turn those intentions into reality.
Have you ever started the week full of good intentions, only to watch them get swallowed up by a flood of urgent emails, surprise meetings, or last-minute plans? You’re definitely not alone.
The real secret to staying on track is proactive planning—actually designing your week ahead of time, so your top priorities and strengths get the attention they deserve.
So, how do you make that happen? It all starts with mapping out your week, hour by hour, using what’s called the 168-hour framework. Instead of waiting for things to fill up your calendar, you schedule your most important activities first.
Think of these as your “anchor events”—those key things like important work projects, family dinners, workouts, or even time for creative hobbies. By putting these anchors on your calendar before anything else, you’re protecting that time. You’re making sure it can’t just get bumped away by last-minute requests.
Let’s break it down into a few simple steps:
First, figure out your top priorities and core strengths for the week.
Next, block out specific time for these activities. Treat them like appointments you can’t miss.
Then, fill in everything else—secondary tasks, meetings, and obligations—around those anchors.
This style of planning is often called “time blocking.” Imagine you’re building a house. You start with a strong foundation, then add the walls, and finish with the smaller details. By leading with what matters most, you shape your week around your values, instead of letting it fill up by accident.
Of course, life isn’t always predictable. Flexibility matters. Treat your schedule as a living document—something you can adjust when things change, while still keeping your core priorities front and center. If something gets interrupted, don’t just toss it out—see if you can reschedule it.
Here’s another great strategy: group similar tasks together. This helps you avoid the mental whiplash of jumping between totally different activities. Maybe you answer all your emails in one focused block, or run all your errands in a single trip. Suddenly, you’ve freed up bigger chunks of time for deep work, or for connecting with people who matter.
A few extra tips for intentional planning:
Try reviewing your upcoming week every Sunday. It’s a chance to make tweaks and set yourself up for success.
Leave some open space for rest, fun, and unexpected opportunities.
And at the end of the week, take a moment to reflect—what worked well, and what could you do better next time?
When you approach your week this way, it stops being a random pile of disconnected tasks. Instead, you build something meaningful and coherent.
The real reward isn’t just getting more done—it’s feeling that sense of control and satisfaction that comes from living out your values and strengths, instead of just reacting to whatever comes your way.
